title: Print advert: an electric bicycle
stem:
[Image description: a full-page photograph. A woman in a tailored suit rides an electric bicycle past a long line of stationary cars on a grey, rain-wet city street. She is lit by a shaft of warm sunlight and looks straight at the camera, smiling. The cars are slightly blurred and tinted blue-grey.]

HEADLINE (large white capitals across the top): STILL WAITING?

BODY COPY (small text, bottom left): Every morning, the average city commuter loses 47 minutes to traffic. That's four working weeks a year, gone. VOLTA e-bikes glide past the queue at up to 25 km/h, charge from any socket, and fold in seconds. Arrive fresher. Arrive faster. Arrive first.

LOGO AND SLOGAN (bottom right, green): VOLTA. Move ahead.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Analyse how the visual features of the advert position the viewer to see the e-bike as a superior choice.
markscheme: contrast/juxtaposition between the moving rider and stationary queue of cars dramatises freedom vs being stuck
warm light on the rider vs cold blue-grey cars: colour symbolism links the product with energy and optimism and cars with gloom
direct gaze and smile create a 'demand', inviting the viewer to identify with her success/confidence
tailored suit targets professional commuters and associates the bike with status, not just leisure
blur on cars vs sharp focus on rider gives her salience and suggests speed
green logo connotes environmental friendliness / 'go'
parts.notes: Reward answers that link each visual choice to the implied audience and purpose rather than listing features.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Examine how the language of the headline, body copy and slogan works to persuade the target audience.
markscheme: rhetorical question 'STILL WAITING?' addresses the viewer directly and implies frustration with their current routine
statistic '47 minutes' / 'four working weeks' (logos) reframes small daily losses as a large, shocking cost
'gone' as a short, final word adds pathos/regret
verb 'glide' connotes ease and effortlessness compared with the jammed queue
tricolon and anaphora 'Arrive fresher. Arrive faster. Arrive first.' builds rhythm and climaxes in competitive advantage
slogan 'Move ahead' has a double meaning: physical movement and career/social progress
practical details (charge from any socket, folds) address likely objections

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate how effectively the advert as a whole addresses its intended audience.
markscheme: identifies the audience precisely (urban professional commuters frustrated by traffic)
judges effectiveness of image–text interaction, e.g. headline anchors the image's meaning
considers a limitation, e.g. the statistic is unattributed / glamorised image ignores rain, safety or cost
reaches a reasoned overall judgement supported by references
parts.notes: Evaluation must weigh strengths against limitations; unsupported praise scores low.

title: Blog post: the last video shop
stem:
THE REWIND DIARIES — Post #212

So. It's happened. Frames, the little video shop on Carver Street, closes on Friday.

I know what you're thinking. Video shop? In this decade? Fair. But hear me out.

For eleven years, Mr Osei has stood behind that counter, under a flickering neon sign that has spelt 'FRAM S' since 2019. He knows that Mrs Lindqvist wants a musical every Thursday. He knows that the twins from number 40 will argue for twenty minutes and then rent the same horror film again. He knows my name, which is more than I can say for my streaming account, which keeps recommending documentaries about sharks because I watched one, once, at 2 a.m.

Algorithms know what we clicked. Mr Osei knew what we meant.

On Friday, I'm going to rent one last film. I don't even own a player anymore. I'll buy one if I have to.

If you're local, come. Bring someone. Tell him what he got right.

(Comments are open. Tell me about your Frames.)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Analyse how the blogger creates a personal voice and a relationship with readers.
markscheme: conversational register: 'So.', 'Fair.', 'hear me out' imitates speech and builds intimacy
anticipates reader's scepticism ('I know what you're thinking') – direct address draws readers into dialogue
self-deprecating humour about shark documentaries makes the persona likeable and relatable
minor sentences and short paragraphs suit online reading and create a hesitant, emotional rhythm
closing imperatives ('come', 'Bring someone') and open comments use blog conventions to build community
specific named details (Mrs Lindqvist, the twins) create authenticity / ethos of a local insider

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Examine how the text represents the contrast between human relationships and digital technology.
markscheme: the anecdotes about regulars present Mr Osei as attentive and knowing
the streaming service is personified ironically as failing to know the blogger despite data
antithesis 'Algorithms know what we clicked. Mr Osei knew what we meant.' crystallises the contrast between data and understanding
past tense 'knew' signals loss / elegiac tone
the broken neon sign 'FRAM S' is a symbol of decline yet affectionate imperfection
gesture of buying a player shows commitment to human connection over convenience
evaluation: representation is nostalgic and one-sided; omits the conveniences of streaming

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Discuss how the structure of the post contributes to its purpose.
markscheme: opening minor sentence 'So.' and the news of closure create an immediate hook
middle section builds through accumulating examples (anaphora 'He knows') to an emotional climax
the one-line antithesis is isolated in its own paragraph for emphasis
ending moves from reflection to call to action and comment invitation, turning private grief into collective response
